M2|baseline|run1.question: What approaches do papers in this collection use to enforce safety constraints while a learning agent or robot controller is acting?
M2|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts describe two main enforcement approaches:

1. **A controller monitor / shield that intercepts actions**
   - In VSRL, the system does offline verification and then uses a controller monitor during exploration: “**Safe exploration with controller monitor**” and “**whenever an action is attempted, the object detector and safety monitor**” are used to decide whether to allow it [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5].
   - The figure text says the monitor checks: “**Is at safe?**” and, if not, it performs a “**Substitute safe action**” instead of the attempted one [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5].

2. **Shielding / backup controller override**
   - The human-interactive control paper says the algorithm “**builds on shielding**” and “**takes as input an arbitrary controller**” and “**combines it with backup controller**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.2].
   - It “**uses on-the-fly verification based on abstract interpretation to determine whether it is safe modulo fault to use the given controller; if so, it uses the given controller, but otherwise, it uses a backup controller**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.2].

More broadly, the papers emphasize:
- **Offline verification plus run-time monitoring**: VSRL performs “**Offline verification and controller monitor synthesis**” before safe exploration begins [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5].
- **Abstract interpretation for conservative safety checking**: one paper says, “**We use abstract interpretation to conservatively overapproximate the reachable set of the system**” and ensure safety with respect to that overapproximation [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.1].

So, from these excerpts, safety is enforced by **monitoring/shielding actions at runtime**, often using **offline verification** or **on-the-fly verification with abstract interpretation**, and **replacing unsafe actions with safe backup actions** when needed.

M3|baseline|run1.question: How do papers in this collection use program analysis or synthesis to improve applications that run against a database?
M3|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts show several ways these papers use program analysis or synthesis to improve database-backed applications:

1. **Translate imperative application logic into SQL that runs in the database.**  
   One paper says QBS “**automatically converts portions of it into SQL expressions that run in the database**” after analyzing the code [DBLP_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.1]. The same excerpt explains that this lets developers keep writing code as usual while moving work into the DBMS: “**developers using transparent persistence frameworks [can] continue writing applications as usual**” and QBS “**retains the best of both worlds**” [DBLP_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.1].

2. **Use program analysis and synthesis to move functionality between application and database layers.**  
   StatusQuo is described as using “**program analysis and program synthesis to enable the seamless movement of functionality between the database and application layers**” [DBLP_conf_cidr_CheungAMSM13 p.1]. It “**takes the functionality that was originally written as imperative code and translati[es] it into relational queries that execute in the database**” [DBLP_conf_cidr_CheungAMSM13 p.1]. It also “**makes runtime decisions about the optimal placement of computation, in order to reduce data movement between the database and application server**” [DBLP_conf_cidr_CheungAMSM13 p.1].

3. **Holistically optimize the runtime system and DBMS.**  
   The survey-style article says prior work “**analyz[es] the application program, the runtime system, and the DBMS as a whole**” and uses “**various program analysis and database optimization**” to produce “**order-of-magnitude speedups in real-world database applications**” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.2]. It also says the article’s projects “**holistically optimize both the runtime system and the DBMS**” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.2].

4. **Reduce round trips and data movement by partitioning code and batching queries.**  
   The same article says PYXIS uses analysis of “**the DBMS and application server together**” to “**generate program partitionings specialized for each profile**” and thereby improve “**performance and scalability**” without requiring workload-specific manual decisions [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.8]. It also says query batching uses “**static program analysis to extract queries that will be executed unconditionally by a single client**” and execute them “**asynchronously in a single round trip**” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.8].

Overall, the collection uses program analysis/synthesis to **push computation into the database, choose where computation should run, batch database interactions, and optimize the combined application–DBMS system** [DBLP_conf_cidr_CheungAMSM13 p.1; DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.2; DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.8].

systems researchers have developed specialized compilers and runtime systems for hosting applications.
However, there has been relatively little work that optimizes database applications by considering these
specialized systems in combination and looking for optimization opportunities that span across them.
In this article, we highlight three projects that optimize database applications by looking at both the

It would be interesting to use PYXIS to partition larger programs, and the same technique to other application

4 Batching DBMS Interactions
PYXIS shows that reducing round trips between the application and database servers can improve application
performance significantly. Query batching is another common technique to reduce such round trips. For instance,
many ORM libraries allow developers annotate their code to prefetch extra persistent objects before such objects
are needed by the program. Unfortunately, deciding when and what objects to prefetch is difficult, especially
when developers do not know how the results that are returned by their methods will be used.
There is prior research that uses static program analysis to extract queries that will be executed uncondi-
tionally by a single client in the application [16, 23, 22]. The extracted queries are executed asynchronously

current SLOTH prototype.
5 Conclusion
In this article, we described three projects that improve the performance of database applications. We showed
that by co-optimizing the runtime system and the DBMS, we can achieve a speedup of multiple orders of
magnitude in application performance. We believe that the techniques presented are complementary to each
other. In future work, we plan to investigate combining these techniques and measuring the overall performance
improvement using real-world applications.
The idea of co-optimization across different software systems opens up new opportunities in both program-
ming systems and database research. For instance, it would be interesting to apply program partitioning to other
application domains that involve multiple systems, such as partitioning code and data among web clients, appli-
cation servers, and the DBMS. In addition, techniques used in QBS can also be used to build new optimizing
compilers: for instance, converting code to make use of specialized routines such as MapReduce or machine
learning libraries.

M4|baseline|run1.question: How is faceted execution used in this collection to enforce information flow policies?
M4|baseline|run1.answer:
Faceted execution is used as a dynamic enforcement mechanism that represents sensitive data with different “facets” for different viewers, so one execution can simulate multiple security-relevant executions.

From the Jeeves paper excerpt:

- It “**extend[s] Jeeves with faceted values**,” which “**exploit the structure of sensitive values**” and “**yield both greater expressiveness**” while helping “**reasoning about runtime behavior**” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.1].
- The system is designed so that “**a single execution with faceted values is equivalent to multiple different executions without faceted values**” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7].
- This equivalence is used to ensure security: “**we also prove that the system cannot leak sensitive information either via the output or by the choice of output channel**” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7].
- The mechanism chooses an appropriate viewing context / program counter for output: “**A program counter pc is chosen such that the policies are satisfied, which determines the channel f and the value to print R**” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7].

From the Jacqueline / λJDB excerpt:

- The faceted execution semantics “**describe the propagation of labels and facets for the purpose of complying with policies at computation sinks**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.7].
- For database operations, a row inconsistent with the current program counter is ignored, and a consistent row produces “**a faceted expression that appears like V′′ to principals that can see the B-labeled row and like V′ to other principals**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.7].
- The collection also says the framework provides “**termination-insensitive non-interference and policy compliance**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.2].

So, in this collection, faceted execution enforces information flow policies by encoding policy-dependent views directly into the runtime values and by ensuring that outputs and channels are selected only in ways that satisfy the active policies.

M5|baseline|run1.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts show refinement types being used for several things:

- **To distinguish program terms from refinement terms and express predicates in types.** The paper says, “λL distinguishes between program terms t and refinement terms r, used inside types” and that “types include refined base types and function types” with refinements as “a refinement predicate over the program variables and a special value variable ν” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

- **To specify programs and policies, especially for synthesis.** One paper says, “Using refinement types as an interface to synthesis” and discusses that they can specify programs with “nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5]. Another says the work combines “refinement type inference” with “synthesis of recursive functional programs” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16].

- **To guide program synthesis through type checking and abduction.** The synthesis paper describes “leveraging bidirectional type checking for synthesis” and using constraints to “discover” information during synthesis [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16], and another excerpt mentions “round-trip type checking” that propagates requirements top-down and enables “the abduction of the branch condition” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

- **To express richer properties through abstract refinements.** One excerpt says “extending the type system with abstract refinements allows us to express a wider class of properties” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

- **To support information-flow control.** The title and text of the first paper indicate “Liquid Information Flow Control” and discuss labels as refinement terms [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used to **encode program properties and policies in types, guide synthesis, and represent security/information-flow constraints** [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16].

M6|baseline|run1.question: How do 'Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly', the Euler system, and ReaS each make numerical optimization work on programs?
M6|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts say that all three approaches make numerical optimization more workable by **replacing or approximating the original program with a smoother function** so that local search methods can operate better, but they emphasize this idea in slightly different ways.

1. **“Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly”**  
   It says smooth interpretation “facilitates the use of local numerical search techniques (e.g., gradient descent)” by taking “the convolution of the program with a Gaussian function,” which “effectively replac[es] discontinuous switches in the program by continuous transitions” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11 p.1]. It also notes that “Exact Gaussian smoothing of programs is undecidable,” so implementations must be approximate [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11 p.1].

2. **Euler**  
   Euler’s “algorithmic core” is “smooth interpretation,” described as “a scheme for approximating a program by a series of smooth mathematical functions,” and “it is these smooth approximations that are used as the targets of numerical optimization” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.1]. The paper further explains that “Applying Gaussian convolution to this function gives us a smooth function,” and that “β controls the extent of smoothing: higher values of β lead to greater smoothing and easier numerical search” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.4]. Euler “negotiates this tradeoff by starting with a moderately high value of β, optimizing the resultant smooth function, then iteratively reducing β and refining the search results” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.4].

3. **ReaS**  
   ReaS also uses smoothing, saying that its “first important feature” is “the ability to use numerical optimization by performing automatic differentiation on a smooth approximation of the program” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.4]. It says “Smoothing can ameliorate the problems inherent in numerical search” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.4]. ReaS then adds a SAT-based component: “The ReaS approach is to turn the SMT paradigm on its head,” and it aims to use a SAT solver to “eliminate local solutions” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.4].

So, in short:

- **Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly**: uses **Gaussian convolution** to replace discontinuities with continuous transitions [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11 p.1].
- **Euler**: uses **smooth interpretation / smooth approximations** as optimization targets, with a tunable smoothing parameter β [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.1; p.4].
- **ReaS**: uses **a smooth approximation plus automatic differentiation**, and combines that with **SAT solving to eliminate local solutions** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.4].

M7|baseline|run1.question: How does Stitch's approach to library learning differ from DreamCoder's?
M7|baseline|run1.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder mainly in how it searches and what it optimizes:

- DreamCoder “learns libraries iteratively”: it starts with “a low-level DSL,” then “alternates between synthesizing programs … and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].
- Stitch instead “synthesizes the maximally-compressive abstraction for a corpus of programs through a branch-and-bound top-down search,” using “an upper bound on the compression of any partially-constructed abstraction to guide and prune the search” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].
- The paper also contrasts their objective handling: DreamCoder “implements a probabilistic Bayesian objective for judging candidate abstractions,” while “Stitch … effectively judges compression quality” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.25].
- In terms of practical behavior, Stitch is described as “an anytime algorithm that can be stopped early for a best-so-far result,” whereas DreamCoder is treated as the baseline iterative system [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

So, in short: DreamCoder learns libraries iteratively via neurally-guided program synthesis plus library updates, while Stitch uses a top-down branch-and-bound search to directly find highly compressive abstractions, with better efficiency [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.17][DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

M8|baseline|run1.question: How do the automated feedback system for introductory programming assignments and sk_p differ in how they correct student programs?
M8|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts indicate that the two systems correct student programs in different ways:

- The automated feedback system for introductory programming assignments uses an explicit error model and computes “minimal corrections” to a student’s incorrect solution. It says, “the system automatically derives minimal corrections to student’s incorrect solutions” and “uses an error model describing the potential corrections and constraint-based synthesis to compute minimal corrections to student’s incorrect solutions” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1] [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.10].

- sk_p instead learns from past correct programs and uses a very local context model. The excerpt says, “a model learned from past correct programs is used to correct future incorrect programs” [DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.9], and that “At each correction site, the model only uses one statement before and after the site as context to generate a distribution of corrections” [DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.2]. It also says sk_p “learns short code fragments that appear frequently in correct solutions and identifies fragments in incorrect submissions that look similar” [DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.2].

So, in short: the first system corrects by applying a hand-specified error model and synthesis to find minimal fixes, while sk_p corrects by learning local correction patterns from correct solutions and applying them to incorrect submissions.

It then “**train[s] a pair of models, a policy that proposes the new piece of code to write, and a value function that assesses the prospects of the code written so-far**,” and at test time “**combine[s] these models with a Sequential Monte Carlo algorithm**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.1].

- In the **blended abstract semantics** paper, execution is used to represent partial programs by mixing concrete and learned execution. The paper says it uses “**blended neural execution**” and that “**for functions whose arguments are not fully defined, such as moveHand, we instead employ abstract neural modules to represent the execution state**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.3]. It also explains that “**this combination of learned execution and concrete execution allows robust representation of partial programs**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.3], and more generally that blended abstract semantics “**aims to represent the state of unfinished programs as faithfully as possible by concretely executing program components whenever possible, and otherwise, approximating program state with a learned abstract execution model**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.2].

So, **Write, Execute, Assess** uses a REPL to directly execute partial programs and feed the resulting semantics into a search procedure, while the **blended abstract semantics** paper uses concrete execution where possible and learned abstract execution otherwise to build a representation of partial program state for search.

M12|baseline|run1.question: How do the formula-simplifier paper and the CNF-encoder paper each use synthesis to improve constraint solvers?
M12|baseline|run1.answer:
The two papers use synthesis in different but related ways:

- The formula-simplifier paper says it uses synthesis to automatically create rewrite-based simplifiers for formulas: “by combining machine learning techniques with constraint-based synthesis, it is possible to synthesize a formula simplifier fully automatically from a corpus of representative problems” [DBLP_journals_corr_0002S16 p.1]. It also frames this as tailoring simplification to a domain: “making it possible to create formula simplifiers tailored to specific problem domains” [DBLP_journals_corr_0002S16 p.1].

- The CNF-encoder paper uses synthesis to automatically generate domain-specific SAT/CNF encodings. It says its approach “relies on program synthesis technology, allowing us to symbolically search for an encoding based on a formal specification” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.3]. The goal is to improve solver performance by producing encodings that are “propagation complete and minimal for multiple challenging domains” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.15], and the evaluation says these “domain-specific encodings are able to significantly improve the performance of CVC4” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.3].

So, in short: the first paper synthesizes simplification rules for formulas, while the second synthesizes better CNF encodings; both use synthesis to make constraint-solving more efficient and domain-specific.

M2|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts describe two main approaches for enforcing safety constraints while a learning agent or robot controller is acting:

1. **Shielding / controller overriding for human-interactive robots**  
   The paper says it “**propose[s] an algorithm that overrides an arbitrary given controller as needed to ensure that the robot is safe**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.1]. It also states that “**our algorithm builds on shielding**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.2].  
   In the later example, the shielded controller “**substitute[s] safe action**” when needed [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5], and the result is “**both controllers are always safe**” for the alternative backup-action setting [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.6].

2. **Controller monitor enforcing safe actions during RL exploration**  
   The VSRL paper says that during safe exploration, “**whenever an action is attempted, the object detector and safety monitor ar[...],**” and the figure explains that the system checks, “**Is at safe?**” If not, it says “**Substitute safe action**” and then “**Perform a’**” instead of the original action [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5].  

So, from the excerpts, safety is enforced by **runtime action replacement/override**: a shield or monitor checks attempted actions and substitutes a safe one when necessary [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.1][DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2110-05440 p.2][DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.5].

M3|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts say these papers improve database applications by using analysis/synthesis to move work into the DBMS and optimize the whole stack.

- One paper says that database applications often suffer because “developers must manually determine 1) whether a piece of computation should be executed as a query by the DBMS or as general-purpose code in the application” and that “the compiler and query optimizer optimize parts of the program, but they do not share information” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.1]. It then says the paper’s approach is to “apply[] a mix of declarative database optimization and modern program analysis techniques” and that this can produce “a speedup of multiple orders of magnitude” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.1].

- Another paper proposes QBS, which “automatically identifies fragments of application logic that can be pushed into SQL queries” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.1]. It does this by “automatically synthesizing invariants and postconditions for the original code fragment” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.1].

- The later summary of the same line of work says they “analyzing the application program, the runtime system, and the DBMS as a whole” and applying “program analysis and database optimization to drive program optimizations” to get “order-of-magnitude speedups in real-world database applications” [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.2].

So, in these excerpts, program analysis/synthesis is used to infer what can be pushed to SQL, transform imperative fragments into declarative database queries, and optimize the application, runtime, and DBMS together for large performance gains [DBLP_journals_debu_CheungMSAM14 p.2][DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.1].

M4|updated|run1.question: How is faceted execution used in this collection to enforce information flow policies?
M4|updated|run1.answer:
Faceted execution is used as a way to represent and run a program so that one execution can stand in for multiple policy-specific executions.

The excerpts say that “a single execution with faceted values is equivalent to multiple different executions without faceted values” and that “a single execution with faceted values projects to multiple different executions without faceted values” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7]. This is the core enforcement idea: the program carries “faceted values” that encode both sensitive and insensitive views, and projection yields the view appropriate for a given policy context [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7].

The paper also says they “extend Jeeves with faceted values” to “yield both greater expressiveness and to facilitate reasoning about runtime behavior” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.1]. In the database-backed application setting, they explicitly list “Faceted execution for database-backed applications” as a contribution and say they “present a dynamic semantics for the λJDB core language and proving termination-insensitive non-interference and policy compliance” [DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.2].

So, based on the excerpts, faceted execution enforces information flow policies by:
- representing sensitive data with facets,
- letting one run simulate the different policy-dependent runs,
- and supporting proofs of “non-interference” / “policy compliance” [DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.7; DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.2].

The excerpts do not give a full operational description of the runtime enforcement rules beyond this, but they do state that the runtime “produce[s] outputs adhering to policies” and that faceted execution is used to implement that behavior [DBLP_conf_pldi_YangHASFC16 p.13; DBLP_conf_plas_AustinYFS13 p.1].

M5|updated|run1.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts show refinement types being used for several purposes:

1. **Program synthesis / specifying programs**
   - “**Our work is the first to leverage general decidable refinement types for synthesis**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16]
   - “**Using refinement types, we were able to express** 3 out of 3, 10, 5, and 7 of their most complex benchmarks” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15]

2. **Expressing policies in applications**
   - “we use [dependent function types] **to specify policies in data-centric applications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13]

3. **Refining base types with predicates over program values**
   - “In a refined base types {B |r }, r is a refinement predicate over the program variables and a special value variable ν” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13]

4. **Inferring or checking program properties during synthesis**
   - The synthesis paper describes “**refinement type inference**” as one of the two areas it combines [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16]
   - It also says their solver handles subtype constraints such as “`⊢ α′ <: List β′ | len ν > 0`” and produces Horn constraints [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.11]

5. **Specification where examples would be cumbersome**
   - “For certain functions, providing examples is easy whereas **writing a refinement type is cumbersome** or, due to the limitations of decidable refinement logic, even impossible.” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16]
   - Conversely, “refinement types are concise and intuitive” for some tasks [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15]

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used to **specify and infer program properties, support synthesis, and encode policies**. The excerpts do not provide a broader survey beyond these uses.

M6|updated|run1.question: How do 'Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly', the Euler system, and ReaS each make numerical optimization work on programs?
M6|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts say all three use some form of program approximation or smoothing to make numerical optimization applicable to programs, but they do it in slightly different ways.

- **“Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly”** explains that smooth interpretation “**attenuates such features by taking the convolution of the program with a Gaussian function, effectively replacing discontinuous switches in the program by continuous transitions**” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11 p.1]. It also says the paper provides “**a concrete design for an approximate smooth interpreter**” and that “**SmoothP(x, β) uses an abstract interpreter to approximate P by a pair of simpler programs Pinf and Psup, then performs a symbolic computation on these approximations**” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS11 p.3].

- **Euler** uses this same line of work as its algorithmic core: “**the algorithmic core of Euler is smooth interpretation [1,2], a scheme for approximating a program by a series of smooth mathematical functions. Rather than the original program, it is these smooth approximations that are used as the targets of numerical optimization**” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.1]. It also frames the motivation as the fact that “**branches and loops can cause even simple programs to have highly irregular, ill-conditioned behavior**,” while numerical methods work only in “**relatively smooth search spaces**” [DBLP_conf_cav_ChaudhuriS12 p.1].

- **ReaS** makes programs differentiable by smoothing discrete control: it says ReaS “**makes the program end-to-end differentiable by smoothing any Boolean expression that introduces discontinuity such as conditionals and relaxing the Boolean unknowns so that numerical optimization can be performed**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.1]. It also combines this with search guidance from SAT: “**ReaS uses a SAT solver to help the numerical search overcome local solutions by incrementally fixing values to the Boolean expressions**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.1].

So, in short:
- **Smoothing a Program Soundly and Robustly**: smooths programs via Gaussian convolution and an approximate smooth interpreter.
- **Euler**: uses smooth interpretation so optimization runs over smooth approximations instead of the original program.
- **ReaS**: smooths Boolean/discrete parts to make the program differentiable, then uses SAT to steer numerical search past local optima.

M7|updated|run1.question: How does Stitch's approach to library learning differ from DreamCoder's?
M7|updated|run1.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in that Stitch is described as a “corpus-guided top-down library learning tool” that uses the corpus to “strongly constrain the search space and direct the search towards abstractions that capture the greatest degree of shared syntactic structure” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.3]. In contrast, DreamCoder “learns libraries iteratively”: it starts from “a low-level DSL,” then “alternates between synthesizing programs (via a neurally-guided enumerative search) … and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].

The excerpts also say Stitch is evaluated as a comparison to DreamCoder and that Stitch “learns libraries of comparable quality to those found by the algorithm of Ellis et al. 2021 … while being 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and using 2 orders of magnitude less memory” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.3]. Additionally, Stitch is limited in one way the paper notes: in the list domain it “cannot learn higher-order abstractions,” whereas DreamCoder’s higher-order abstractions are useful there [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.19].

So, based on the excerpts, the main difference is:
- Stitch: corpus-guided, top-down, search-space-constraining library learning [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.3]
- DreamCoder: iterative, enumerative synthesis plus library updating from a low-level DSL [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18]

M8|updated|run1.question: How do the automated feedback system for introductory programming assignments and sk_p differ in how they correct student programs?
M8|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts suggest they differ mainly in **how the correction model is defined and applied**.

For the automated feedback system for introductory programming assignments, the paper says it uses “**a reference implementation of the assignment, and an error model consisting of potential corrections to errors that students might make**” and then “**automatically derives minimal corrections to student’s incorrect solutions**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1]. It also says the technique “**uses an error model describing the potential corrections and constraint-based synthesis to compute minimal corrections**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.10]. The correction search can be large, and “**the program is translated to a sketch by the Sketch Translator**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.3].

By contrast, sk_p is described as learning from data: “**a model learned from past correct programs is used to correct future incorrect programs**” [DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.9]. It is also described as a “**skipgram**” model where “**At each correction site, the model only uses one statement before and after the site as context to generate a distribution of corrections**” and “**learns short code fragments that appear frequently in correct solutions and identifies fragments in incorrect submissions that look similar**” [DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.2].

So, in short: the first system corrects programs by **applying a hand-specified error model and synthesis to find minimal corrections**, while sk_p corrects programs by **learning local fragment-completion patterns from correct student submissions and using those patterns to propose fixes** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.10; DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.2; DBLP_conf_oopsla_PuNSB16 p.9].

M9|updated|run1.question: What do the Fusion 360 Gallery paper and JoinABLe each contribute to learning from CAD designs?
M9|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts show that the two papers contribute to learning from CAD designs in different but related ways.

- **Fusion 360 Gallery** contributes a **dataset and environment for programmatic CAD construction from human design sequences**. It says the paper provides “**Fusion 360 Gallery: A Dataset and Environment for Programmatic CAD Construction from Human Design Sequences**” and that “**The Fusion 360 Gallery reconstruction dataset consists of 8,625 designs**” from real users [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.4]. It also says the dataset is built around a DSL where “**A program consists of a sequence of sketch and extrude operations that iteratively modify the current geometry**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.5]. So its contribution is mainly data and a structured environment for learning CAD reconstruction from human-made sequences.

- **JoinABLe** contributes a **learning-based method for assembling CAD parts into joints**. The paper states, “**we introduce JoinABLe, a learning-based method that assembles parts together to form joints**” and that it “**uses the weak supervision available in standard parametric CAD files without the help of object class labels or human guidance**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1]. It further says JoinABLe is “**our bottom-up approach to assembly that learns how parts connect locally to form parametric CAD joints**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.2]. So its contribution is the method for learning part-to-part assembly from weakly supervised CAD data.

In short: **Fusion 360 Gallery provides the dataset/environment for CAD construction and reconstruction learning, while JoinABLe provides the learning method for bottom-up CAD joint assembly** [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.4][DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1].

M10|updated|run1.question: How do 'Write, Execute, Assess' and the blended abstract semantics paper each use execution to guide program search?
M10|updated|run1.answer:
Both papers use execution as part of the search process, but in different ways.

In **“Write, Execute, Assess”**, execution is provided by a REPL:
- The paper says it “**integrat[es] components which write, execute, and assess code to navigate the search space of possible programs**” and “**equip[s] the search process with an interpreter or a read-eval-print-loop (REPL), which immediately executes partially written programs, exposing their semantics**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.1].
- It further explains that “**The REPL addresses a basic challenge of program synthesis: tiny changes in syntax can lead to huge changes in semantics**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.1].
- The search is then guided by learned models: “**We train a pair of models, a policy that proposes the new piece of code to write, and a value function that assesses the prospects of the code written so-far**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.1].

In the **blended abstract semantics** paper, execution is partly concrete and partly learned:
- It says that “**The sub-expression buildColumn(1) is fully concrete, and can thus be concretely executed to render an image**,” while for incomplete parts, “**we instead employ abstract neural modules to represent the execution state**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.3].
- The paper emphasizes that “**This combination of learned execution and concrete execution allows robust representation of partial programs, which can be used for downstream synthesis tasks**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.3].
- It also describes search using those representations: “**We explore a variety of code-writing search algorithms**,” including “**sample-based search and best-first search**” with policy scores, and “**A*-based search with −log V(s,X) as a heuristic**” when a value function is added [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.6].

So, in short: **Write, Execute, Assess** uses a REPL to execute partial programs directly and guide search with policy/value models, while **blended abstract semantics** uses a mix of concrete execution and learned abstract execution states to represent partial programs for search.

M11|updated|run1.question: How do OmegaC and the random conditional distribution paper each extend probabilistic programming?
M11|updated|run1.answer:
OMEGAC extends probabilistic programming by adding support for counterfactual inference. The excerpt says it is “a probabilistic programming language with support for counterfactual inference” and that it “accomplish[es] this by introducing a new operator to probabilistic programming akin to Pearl’s do” [DBLP_conf_icml_TavaresK0DS21 p.1]. It also says OMEGAC is “a Turing-universal programming language for causal reasoning” that “allows users to automatically derive causal inferences” and “compute counterfactuals” [DBLP_conf_icml_TavaresK0DS21 p.1].

The random conditional distribution paper extends probabilistic programming by adding a construct for distributional inference: “we introduce a probability construct – the random conditional distribution – and incorporate it into a probabilistic programming language Omega” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1903-10556 p.1]. It further explains that this is for “the randomizing and conditioning of distributional properties,” and that Omega “has an operator to construct random conditional distributions as a primitive construct” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1903-10556 p.2].

So, in short: OMEGAC extends probabilistic programming toward counterfactual/causal reasoning, while the random conditional distribution paper extends it toward higher-order distributional inference about properties like expectation and variance [DBLP_conf_icml_TavaresK0DS21 p.1; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1903-10556 p.1].

M12|updated|run1.question: How do the formula-simplifier paper and the CNF-encoder paper each use synthesis to improve constraint solvers?
M12|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts show that both papers use synthesis to generate solver-related components automatically, but for different kinds of solvers.

- In the formula-simplifier paper, the authors say they “show that by combining machine learning techniques with constraint-based synthesis, it is possible to synthesize a formula simplifier fully automatically from a corpus of representative problems, making it possible to create formula simplifiers tailored to specific problem domains” [DBLP_journals_corr_0002S16 p.1]. They also explain that “many applications that rely on solvers often implement their own formula simplification layer” and that formulas from a tool can have “patterns that can be easily exploited by a custom formula simplifier” [DBLP_journals_corr_0002S16 p.1]. So synthesis is used to automatically build domain-specific simplifiers that rewrite formulas before solver use.

- In the CNF-encoder paper, the authors say their approach “relies on program synthesis technology, allowing us to symbolically search for an encoding based on a formal specification” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.3]. They further state that they “are the first ones to generate domain specific encodings that are propagation complete and minimal for multiple challenging domains using program synthesis technology” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.15]. So synthesis is used to automatically generate domain-specific CNF encoders for bit-vector solvers, improving performance: “the resulting domain-specific encodings are able to significantly improve the performance of CVC4 when run in eager bit-blasting mode” [DBLP_conf_sat_Inala0S16 p.3].

In short: the first paper synthesizes formula simplifiers; the second synthesizes CNF encoders. Both aim to improve solver performance by automatically producing domain-specific preprocessing/encoding components.

S2|updated|run1.answer:
The benchmark has **800 Python functions**. The paper says, “**CRUXEval consists of 800 distinct functions**” and “**a benchmark consisting of 800 Python functions (3–13 lines)**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.5] [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.1].

Each function supports **two tasks**:

1. **Output prediction** — “**the goal is to predict the output of executing the function on its associated input**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.5].  
2. **Input prediction** — “**the goal is to find any input such that executing the function on that input produces the output**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.5].

So, in short: **800 functions; the two tasks are input prediction and output prediction** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.1] [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.5].

LINC stands for “Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

It also describes LINC as “a two-stage neurosymbolic approach for logical reasoning tasks” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.2].

S4|updated|run1.question: What are the three pillars of machine programming, and what does each emphasize?
S4|updated|run1.answer:
The three pillars are **intention, invention, and adaptation**. The paper says: “The general goal of machine programming is to remove the burden of writing correct and efficient code from a human programmer and to instead place it on a machine” and then defines the pillars as “(i) intention, (ii) invention, and (iii) adaptation” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

What each emphasizes:

- **Intention**: “the ability of the machine to understand the programmer’s goals through more natural forms of interaction” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2]. The abstract also says, “Intention emphasizes advancements in the human-to-computer and computer-to-machine-learning interfaces” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1].

- **Invention**: “the ability of the machine to discover how to accomplish such goals; whether by devising new algorithms, or even by devising new abstractions from which such algorithms can be built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2]. The abstract says, “Invention emphasizes the creation or refinement of algorithms or core hardware and software building blocks through machine learning (ML)” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1].

- **Adaptation**: “the ability to autonomously evolve software, whether to make it execute efficiently on new or existing platforms, or to fix errors and address vulnerabilities” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2]. The abstract says, “Adaptation emphasizes advances in the use of ML-based constructs to autonomously evolve software” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1].

S6|updated|run1.question: In 'Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis', how is the subset of examples chosen?
S6|updated|run1.answer:
The subset is chosen **iteratively and greedily**.

The paper says the method “**is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.1].

More specifically, it explains that the algorithm “**starts with an empty subset**,” then “**computes the probability of all the examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset**,” and “**adds the least probable example to the subset**” because “**the example with the lowest probability would best prune the search space as a constraint**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.3].

It also gives Algorithm 1, which “**constructs the subset D′ greedily, choosing the example that maximally prunes the solution space**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.3].

Abstract
Program synthesis is a class of regression prob-
lems where one seeks a solution, in the form of
a source-code program, mapping the inputs to
their corresponding outputs exactly. Due to its
precise and combinatorial nature, program syn-
thesis is commonly formulated as a constraint sat-
isfaction problem, where input-output examples
are encoded as constraints and solved with a con-
straint solver. A key challenge of this formulation
is scalability: while constraint solvers work well
with a few well-chosen examples, a large set of ex-
amples can incur significant overhead in both time
and memory. We describe a method to discover
a subset of examples that is both small and rep-
resentative: the subset is constructed iteratively,
using a neural network to predict the probability
of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen
examples in the subset, and greedily adding the
least probable example. We empirically evaluate
the representativeness of the subsets constructed
by our method, and demonstrate such subsets can
significantly improve synthesis time and stability.

N2|updated|run1.question: In the Lynx paper, what problem is the programmatic SAT solver applied to?
N2|updated|run1.answer:
In the Lynx paper, the programmatic SAT solver is applied to **the RNA-folding problem**, specifically **“the RNA secondary structure prediction problem.”** The paper says it is “**Lynx: A Programmatic SAT Solver for the RNA-Folding Problem**” and that “**We demonstrate the benefits of Lynx through a case-study from computational biology, namely, the RNA secondary structure prediction problem**” [DBLP_conf_sat_GaneshOSDRS12 p.1].

It also says, “**Using Lynx we developed the first SAT based tool for solving the RNA-folding prediction problem**” [DBLP_conf_sat_GaneshOSDRS12 p.2].

efficient for the problem-at-hand, and easy to build and maintain. Equally important,

solver.

Pruning techniques are more generally applicable, and are used aggressively by
the enumerative solver compared against in Sect. 5.

transformation [4,5]. In a similar vein, Chaganty et al. use symbolic reasoning to

N3|updated|run1.question: What does the SPARLING method learn, and what does its main theorem state?
N3|updated|run1.answer:
SPARLING is described as learning “extremely sparse activation tensor[s]” representing “sparse and local latent intermediate variables, which we call motifs” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976 p.1]. The abstract also says it is “an end-to-end spatial concept learning” method and that it “uses a new kind of informational bottleneck that enforces levels of activation sparsity unachievable using other techniques” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976 p.1].

Its main theorem is the “Motif Identifiability Theorem,” which “st[ates] that under certain assumptions it is possible to precisely identify these motifs exclusively by reducing end-to-end error” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976 p.1]. The excerpt further clarifies that the theorem is about “a latent intermediate representation output by a local model” rather than identifiable parameters [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976 p.1].

N4|updated|run1.question: In the LINC paper, what limits the setting the authors consider, and what effect does that limitation have?
N4|updated|run1.answer:
The LINC paper says its setting is limited by a **“Narrow scope of logical reasoning task considered”**: “we focus exclusively on one aspect of logical reasoning: **predicting the truth value of a conclusion given a set of natural language premises**” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

It also says this is a setting “where the” premises are part of the experiment, and earlier it explains an important consequence of the translation step: “the translation from natural language to FOL is a lossy process,” so “the information conveyed through the FOL is sometimes a subset of the information in the original premises” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.8]. The effect is that “Removing pieces of crucial information that were on the critical path to deducing True/False may then leave an uncertain conclusion” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.8].

So, the limitation is that they only consider truth-value prediction from natural-language premises, and the effect is that lossy translation can strip crucial information and make conclusions become **Uncertain**.

C1|updated|run1.question: How do different papers in this collection define the program synthesis problem, and where do their definitions disagree?
C1|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts give several related but not identical descriptions of program synthesis.

1. **Synthesis as deriving an implementation from a logical specification**
   - One paper says program synthesis asks “**whether it is possible to derive an executable implementation from a specification of a system given as a logical formula**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].
   - This is a broad, logic-based definition.

2. **Synthesis as finding a program that fits examples exactly**
   - Another paper says program synthesis is “**a special class of regression problems where rather than minimizing the error on an example dataset, one seeks an exact fit of the examples in the form of a program**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].
   - It further says “**The specification is commonly expressed as a set of input-output examples which the candidate program needs to fit exact**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

3. **Syntax-guided synthesis as synthesis plus syntactic constraints**
   - The Fisman et al. preface says that to overcome computational hardness, “**some syntactic set of constraints is given in order to limit the search space of viable solutions**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1], and that this family of approaches is “**now referred to as syntax-guided synthesis**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].

4. **Synthesis in a specific REPL-based setting**
   - The REPL paper describes a concrete task: “**The synthesis task is to find a CSG program that renders to spec**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.2].
   - This is narrower and framed around rendering to a specification in a graphics language.

### Where they disagree
The main disagreement is about **what form the specification takes**:

- Fisman et al. define synthesis using a **logical formula**: “a specification of a system given as a logical formula” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].
- Pu et al. define it using **input-output examples**: “a set of input-output examples” that the program must fit exactly [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

These are not necessarily contradictory, but they emphasize different specification styles.

A second difference is scope:

- The Fisman definition is **general and abstract** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].
- The REPL paper gives a **domain-specific instance** (“find a CSG program that renders to spec”) [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.2].

### What the excerpts do not settle
The excerpts do **not** provide a formal contradiction between the papers; they show different emphases:
- logical formulas vs. example sets,
- general synthesis vs. syntax-guided synthesis vs. a graphics-specific synthesis task.

So, based only on these excerpts, the papers differ mainly in **how they characterize the specification input to synthesis**, not in whether synthesis is about producing an executable program from constraints.

C2|updated|run1.question: What different strategies do these papers use to combine language models with formal verification or symbolic reasoning?
C2|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts describe several different ways of combining language models with formal verification or symbolic reasoning:

- **Augmenting language models with external tools.** One excerpt says: “The central idea in this line of research is to augment language models with external tools such as calculators, code interpreters and information retrieval systems” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. It also says these works are divided into “two classes,” and that “the model does not need to learn how” to use the tool in one class [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

- **Autoformalization into a symbolic language.** The same excerpt explains “the idea of automatically translating natural language into structured symbolic representations that programs can reason about” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. It gives examples of translating natural language into theorem-prover languages and into “system specificat[ion] languages such as temporal logic” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

- **Neurosymbolic reasoning with an explicit symbolic component.** For logical reasoning, one excerpt says Zhang et al. “finetune a language model to synthesize potential facts paired with likelihoods and then use a handwritten differentiable symbolic reasoner in order to deduce other facts” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. It also says Weir and Van Durme “train neural ‘entailment’ models to decide if and how a given inference rule applies at each stage” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

- **Self-refinement plus neurosymbolic reasoning.** The excerpt says “Logic-LM employs a self-refinement strategy” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

- **Combining LMs with symbolic reasoning for both logical and arithmetic reasoning.** It says “SATLM studies arithmetic reasoning in addition to logical reasoning, showcasing the versatility of the neurosymbolic approach” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

- **Constraint-based synthesis / symbolic search.** A synthesis paper explains that SyGuS is finding an implementation that satisfies “a semantic constraint given by a logical formula” and “a syntactic constraint given by a grammar” [DBLP_journals_corr_AlurFSS16a p.1]. Another excerpt says the search can be done “in a symbolic manner” by encoding the parameterized program “as a constraint system” [DBLP_conf_snapl_CheungKS15 p.3].

- **Symbolic reasoning to improve sampling-based procedures.** One excerpt says “some researchers have explored ways to use symbolic reasoning to improve sampling-based procedures” and gives as an example “a symbolic smoothing transformation” used with “numerical search for synthesis” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.3].

The excerpts do **not** give a single unified taxonomy of all strategies, but they clearly show: tool augmentation, autoformalization, differentiable symbolic reasoning, neural entailment over inference rules, self-refinement, and constraint-based symbolic synthesis/search.

C4|updated|run1.question: Across these papers, what reasons are given for why program synthesis is computationally hard?
C4|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts give two main reasons.

1. **Program synthesis asks for an executable implementation from a specification, and the problem is inherently hard depending on the formalism.**  
   The preface says program synthesis asks “**whether it is possible to derive an executable implementation from a specification of a system given as a logical formula**,” and that “**The exact complexity of the problem depends on the type of the logical formalism and the corresponding type of systems and is either undecidable or of very high computational complexity**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].

2. **The search space is huge, so approaches add syntactic constraints to restrict it.**  
   The same excerpt explains that to address “**the computational hardness**,” researchers added “**some syntactic set of constraints ... in order to limit the search space of viable solutions**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].  
   Another paper similarly describes syntax-guided synthesis as starting with “**a structural hypothesis describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates until it finds a solution**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2], which indicates the difficulty comes from searching candidate programs.

3. **Some synthesis procedures rely on explicit or symbolic search, both of which must explore difficult candidate spaces.**  
   The Jeon et al. excerpt says systems use either “**explicit search—either stochastically or systematically enumerating the candidate program space—and others use symbolic search—encoding the search space as constraints that are solved using a SAT solver**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]. This supports the idea that the hardness comes from the large candidate space and constraint solving.

So, across the excerpts, program synthesis is described as computationally hard because it is a search problem over candidate programs, and because its exact complexity can be “undecidable” or “very high” depending on the specification formalism [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].

C5|updated|run1.question: How do papers in this collection use reinforcement learning in connection with programs or policies?
C5|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts show several ways reinforcement learning is connected to programs or policies:

1. **RL policies made more verifiable by using simpler program structures**
   - One paper says it aims to learn policies whose properties “such as safety, stability, and robustness can be efficiently verified,” and explains that it “focus[es] on learning decision tree policies” because they are “highly structured, making them easy to verify” [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1].
   - It also notes that “decision tree policies achieves performance equal to that of the original DNN policy” in the examples mentioned [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1].

2. **RL policies as programmatic state machines**
   - Another paper proposes “learning programmatic state machine policies that can capture repeating behaviors” [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].
   - It says these policies can “generalize to instances requiring an arbitrary number of repetitions,” which the authors call “inductive generalization” [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].
   - The paper further says it uses “a learning framework called adaptive teaching” to learn such a state machine policy [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].

3. **RL constrained by safe controller programs/filters**
   - A safety-focused paper describes “construct[ing] safety monitors (which we also call safe actions filters in this paper) for reinforcement learning algorithms over a symbolic state space” [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.12].
   - It explains that the monitor is tied to a specification of the form “P →[{ctrl; plant}∗]Q” and that the control program has the form “?P1; a1 ∪···∪Pn; an,” where the actions correspond to the RL agent’s action space [DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.12].

4. **RL using skills as higher-level policies/actions**
   - A 2024 paper explains that “skills” are “a high-level action — such as a fixed sequence of actions (macroaction) or a sub-policy with a termination condition (option)” [DBLP_conf_icml_LiPS24 p.1].
   - It says that “incorporating skills into the agent’s action space (hierarchical RL) allows it to act at a higher level and reach goals in fewer steps” [DBLP_conf_icml_LiPS24 p.1].

5. **Papers benchmarking RL policies and baselines**
   - Bench-Push includes RL baselines such as “Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)” and “Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO),” and these were “trained across all tasks” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.7].

So, in this collection, reinforcement learning is used to learn or evaluate **policies**, and those policies are often represented or constrained as **decision trees, state machines, control programs, safe action filters, or skills** [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1; DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1; DBLP_conf_hybrid_HuntFMHDS21 p.12; DBLP_conf_icml_LiPS24 p.1; DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.7].

Deep reinforcement learning has successfully solved a number of challenging

C6|updated|run1.question: What roles do partial or incomplete programs play across these papers?
C6|updated|run1.answer:
Across these excerpts, partial or incomplete programs are presented as the central object that synthesis methods must represent, evaluate, and search over.

- In the ICLR paper, partial programs matter because synthesis must “represent the behavior of a partially written program before it can be executed, to judge if it is on the right track and predict where to search next” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.1].
- The same paper says the key challenge is “representing the semantics of unfinished code” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.2].
- It explains that incomplete programs guide search, but “Concrete semantics cannot be used for this selection, because expressions such as x + HOLE are incomplete and cannot be executed” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.4].
- Therefore, partial programs are used as candidates in top-down search: “starting with the top-level (incomplete) expression HOLE, we consider all possible expansions” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.4].
- The paper also frames partial programs as something to be analyzed by an alternative semantics: “Conventional abstract interpretation solves this problem by defining an alternative semantics for which even incomplete expressions can be evaluated” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.4].
- More specifically, the abstract says the method represents partial programs with “a flexible combination of concrete execution state and learned neural representations, using the learned approximate semantics when concrete semantics are not known (in unfinished parts of the program)” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.1].
- And it summarizes the role of the approach as “a novel method for representing the semantic state of partially written programs inspired by abstract interpretation” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.3].

One excerpt about MeMo does not discuss partial programs at all; it is about “positive transfer benefits of MeMo” and “noise injection” [DBLP_conf_nips_Tjandrasuwita0S24 p.24].

C7|updated|run1.question: What different ways do these papers evaluate whether a synthesized program is correct?
C7|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts describe several different correctness/evaluation criteria for synthesized programs:

1. **SMT-based formal verification against specifications**
   - One paper says tools “use pre- and post-conditions (and data structure invariants) to describe computations, and rely on unbounded, SMT-based verification to validate candidate programs” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15].
   - It also says these tools “provide the same correctness guarantees as SYNQUID” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15].

2. **Synthesis-time / enumeration-time feasibility**
   - In the sketch-learning paper, training depends on whether sketches can be synthesized into a program “in less than time t” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19 p.4].
   - They “do not run synthesis during training” but instead use likelihood to upper-bound search time, since “search time … can be upper bounded using the likelihood” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19 p.4].

3. **Quantitative objectives for noisy/probabilistic specifications**
   - The metric program synthesis paper says quantitative objectives are used “to deal with noisy or probabilistic specifications” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2206-06164 p.23].
   - It contrasts this with using them “to perform search more effectively” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2206-06164 p.23].

4. **Checking multiple candidate outputs and selecting the best-scoring one**
   - In the CAD joint paper, during training they “calculate the loss from the single network prediction against each ground truth joint pose and take the minimum” because “Any ground truth pose is considered correct” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.28].
   - During evaluation they “compare over multiple ground truth poses and take the joint pose prediction with the lowest CD” (Chamfer Distance) [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.28].

What the excerpts do **not** give is a single unified notion of “correctness” shared by all papers; instead, they show different papers using formal verification, synthesis-time bounds, probabilistic ranking, or metric-based comparison against multiple ground truths.

C8|updated|run1.question: Where do these papers disagree about whether language models genuinely understand the code they produce?
C8|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts do not show a direct disagreement; they mostly align.

What they say is that models can produce code but often do not understand it deeply:

- The ACL paper says code language models have “**a shallow understanding of these counterfeit samples**” and that “**counterfeits from a given model are just as confusing to the model itself as they are to other models**” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].
- Its conclusion says models “**often cannot assess their correctness, reason about their execution, and struggle to repair them**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13].
- The software-engineering survey similarly points to “**a lack of semantic understanding**” and gives a failure case where a model “**generates the function as convert camel to snake, which however does not match the larger codebase**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.21].

The only potentially contrasting note is that some cited prior work suggests limited or mixed understanding:
- “**Jin and Rinard (2023) provide evidence that LMs can learn meaningful representations when trained on programs**” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.8].
- “**West et al. (2023) and Oh et al. (2024) argue that generative capability may not be contingent on understanding capability in textual domains**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13].

But the excerpts themselves do not present one paper claiming genuine understanding while another denies it. Instead, they consistently argue that surface-level generation is not the same as deep understanding.

T1|updated|run1.question: How did the stated motivation for program synthesis change between the earliest and the most recent work in this collection?
T1|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts show an early motivation centered on **constructing programs that satisfy a given specification**. For example, the 2017 paper says: “**Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification**” and describes syntax-guided synthesis as searching for candidates until it “**finds a solution**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]. The 2018 paper likewise frames synthesis around helping with “**the intention challenges**” and using multi-modal specification to “**unambiguously describ[e] complex functionality**” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.3].

The most recent excerpt shifts the motivation toward **learning reusable abstractions from a corpus of programs**. The 2023 paper says: “**Recent work shares Stitch’s goal of learning libraries of program abstractions which capture reusable structure across a corpus of programs**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.26].

So, based on these excerpts, the motivation changed from **synthesizing a correct program from a specification / intent** to **learning reusable program libraries that capture shared structure across many programs** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2; DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.26].

T3|updated|run1.question: How has the role of large language models in program synthesis changed over the period covered by this collection?
T3|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts suggest a shift from **using language models as code generators** toward **using them in broader evaluation and synthesis workflows, while also recognizing their limitations**.

Early on, one excerpt frames program synthesis as a setting where models are directly used to generate programs: it cites **“Program synthesis with large language models”** among related work on code models [DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.9]. Another excerpt emphasizes a key benefit of synthesis itself: **“When a correct program is found, it trivially generalizes correctly to arbitrary query inputs”** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562 p.6]. This contrasts synthesis with neural translation, where **“approaches which attempt to neurally translate directly from inputs to outputs struggle to generate sequences much longer than those seen during training”** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562 p.6].

More recent excerpts show a broader and more critical perspective on LLMs for code. One paper says that existing benchmarks are no longer sufficient and that they suffer from **“data contamination, overfitting, saturation, and focus on merely code generation”** [DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25 p.1]. It introduces a benchmark that goes **“beyond just code generation”** to include **“self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction”** [DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25 p.1]. Another recent excerpt also notes practical limits in evaluating code models: **“due to budget constraints, we only evaluate these two models on a limited subset of our counterfeit datasets”** [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.10].

So, based on these excerpts, the role of LLMs in program synthesis has changed from an initially promising tool for direct code/program generation to one component of a more nuanced ecosystem in which researchers also study generalization, robustness, self-repair, and evaluation limitations.

T4|updated|run1.question: What is the most recent work in this collection on code benchmarks, and how does it differ from earlier benchmarks?
T4|updated|run1.answer:
The most recent work in this collection is **“Challenges and Paths Towards AI for Software Engineering”** and, within the excerpt, specifically its discussion of **evaluation and benchmarks** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.14]. It says:

- “**Today’s code LLM evaluations focus on a narrow set of tasks, suffer from potential contamination, and do not reliably measure real-world software engineering abilities**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.14].
- It also notes that “**HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests, and LiveCodeBench are all at function-level scope**” and that “**Current coding evaluations primarily focus on the code generation task**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.14].

Compared with earlier benchmarks in the excerpts, the differences are:

- **Earlier benchmarks were narrow and code-generation-centric.** The LiveCodeBench excerpt says that “**current benchmarks like HUMANEVAL and MBPP paint a misleading picture**” because “**these benchmarks only focus on code generation, thus overlooking broader code-related capabilities**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25 p.1].
- **Contamination was already a concern earlier.** LiveCodeBench also says benchmarks “**suffer from contamination or overfitting, as benchmark samples are present in the training datasets**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25 p.1].
- **Some earlier benchmarks targeted more specific reasoning/execution tasks.** CRUXEval introduces “**a benchmark consisting of 800 Python functions**” with “**two natural tasks: input prediction and output prediction**” and reports that “**many recent high-scoring models on HumanEval show no improvements on our benchmark**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024 p.1].
- **Other older benchmark efforts were broader in benchmark count or domain, but not necessarily code-specific.** For example, MANTRA created “**a benchmark suite with 285 diverse benchmarks across 6 domains**” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.2], and SyGuS-Comp’15 sampled “**309 benchmarks for the General Track**” plus other tracks [DBLP_journals_corr_AlurFSS16 p.5].

So, based on the excerpts, the most recent work emphasizes that prior code benchmarks were too narrow, often focused on function-level code generation, and vulnerable to contamination, whereas the newer discussion calls for evaluations that better measure real software engineering ability and broader task diversity [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.14; DBLP_conf_iclr_JainHGLYZWSSS25 p.1].

T5|updated|run1.question: Over time, have the papers in this collection moved toward or away from requiring formal specifications?
T5|updated|run1.answer:
The excerpts suggest the papers have moved **toward requiring formal specifications, or at least toward treating them as an increasingly important direction**.

Supporting quotes:

- The ICML excerpt says that because “natural language prompts” are ambiguous, “**One direction to address this limitation is to train models to leverage enhanced specifications with more precise and verifiable representations, such as formal specifications and test-based specifications**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuJLSESS25 p.50].
- The survey excerpt repeats the same idea: “**One direction to address this limitation is to train models to leverage enhanced specifications with more precise and verifiable representations, such as formal specifications and test-based specifications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.33].
- It also explicitly frames this as a collaboration direction: “**Training the next generation of code LLMs needs to account for human-AI collaboration**” and “**learning to leverage specifications beyond natural language through formal methods and user-specified tests can mitigate vague specifications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.33].
- The later FMCAD excerpt says prior methods are “**limited by ambiguous and missing behavioral constraints**,” and describes structured artifacts such as “**formal_results.json**,” “**properties.json**,” and “**tracelinks.json**” for “**traceability**” [DBLP_conf_fmcad_AlurBJMRSSSTU13 p.1; p.3].

So, based on these excerpts, the trend is **away from relying only on natural language and toward more formal, structured, and verifiable specifications**.  

What the excerpts do **not** show is a long-term historical trend across many years or papers; they only show a consistent direction in the cited works.

an approach for the rapid development of high-performance ap-
plications. This approach allows a programmer to write clean and
portable reference code, and then obtain a high-quality implemen-
tation by simply sketching the outlines of the desired implemen-

details while also ensuring that a completed sketch is faithful to
the input reference code. In this paper, we develop StreamBit as
a sketching methodology for the important class of bit-streaming
programs (e.g., coding and cryptography).
A sketch is a partial specification of the implementation, and as
such, it affords several benefits to programmer in terms of produc-
tivity and code robustness. First, a sketch is easier to write com-

Abstract
We present CRUXEval (Code Reasoning, Understanding, and eXecution Evaluation),
a benchmark consisting of 800 Python functions (3-13 lines). Each function comes
with an input-output pair, leading to two natural tasks: input prediction and output
prediction. First, we propose a generic recipe for generating our execution benchmark
which can be used to create future variation of the benchmark. Second, we evaluate
twenty code models on our benchmark and discover that many recent high-scoring
models on HumanEval do not show the same improvements on our benchmark. Third,
we show that simple CoT and fine-tuning schemes can improve performance on our
benchmark but remain far from solving it. The best setup, GPT-4 with chain of thought
(CoT), achieves a pass@1 of 75% and 81% on input and output prediction, respectively.
In contrast, Code Llama 34B achieves a pass@1 of 50% and 46% on input and output
prediction, highlighting the gap between open and closed source models. As no model

3 Benchmark Construction
CRUXEval consists of 800 distinct functions, each with an input-output pair such that executing
the function on the input deterministically produces the output. Using these functions and input-
output pairs, we derive two benchmark tasks. In the output prediction task, the goal is to predict
the output of executing the function on its associated input. In the input prediction task, the goal is
to find any input such that executing the function on that input produces the output. For both
tasks, we use an execution-based correctness metric. For input prediction, a generated input passes
if assert f(generated input) == output passes, and for output prediction, a generated output
passes if assert f(input) == generated output passes. A few statistics about the samples of
CRUXEval can be found in Appendix A.3.
3.1 Generating Candidates
We use Code Llama 34B to generate all the candidate functions and inputs of CRUXEval. To do
so, we prompt it with the name of a function in the Python standard library such as str.zfill
and ask it to generate a Python function that makes use of the library function in addition to 5
test inputs. We provide two varying few-shot examples in our prompt for improved diversity of
generations (see Appendix A.2 for more details). A sample prompt is shown in Listing 11.

Abstract
Program synthesis is a class of regression prob-
lems where one seeks a solution, in the form of
a source-code program, mapping the inputs to
their corresponding outputs exactly. Due to its
precise and combinatorial nature, program syn-
thesis is commonly formulated as a constraint sat-
isfaction problem, where input-output examples
are encoded as constraints and solved with a con-

and memory. We describe a method to discover
a subset of examples that is both small and rep-

using a neural network to predict the probability
of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen
examples in the subset, and greedily adding the
least probable example. We empirically evaluate
the representativeness of the subsets constructed
by our method, and demonstrate such subsets can
significantly improve synthesis time and stability.

proposed program approximation scheme that facilitates the use of local

popular signal-processing technique used to filter noise and discontinu-
